match_note: The first-round reports describe the same content as arXiv v1: the inelastic phonon gap, the two in-gap peaks in Fig. 3a with linear B-field shifts, tip-height (electric-field) tuning, and the DFT orbital moments. The rebuttal quotes new Methods text that v1 lacks: WKB Eqs. 9–11 with tunnelling-probability estimates, the dynamical Coulomb blockade argument, Landau-level and quantum-dot exclusions, citations of Ge et al., and achievable device fields. In v1, Eq. 9 is instead the δh relation and ref. [62] is Black & Welser, so the reference numbering also differs. v1 therefore looks like the submitted, pre-revision manuscript. The only mismatch is that R1 writes 'interface' where the v1 title says 'interphase', probably a typo.

concerns.quote: an examination of the graphitic phonon spectra shows that there are no K phonons at this energy... Other authors... have also interpreted as a dynamical Coulomb suppression gap.
concerns.summary: The soft gap may not be a phonon-assisted inelastic gap, since no K-point phonons exist at that energy, and could instead be a dynamical Coulomb blockade gap.

concerns.quote: All the results stem from two relatively very small features compared to the main spectra intensity... It seems somewhat a stretch to make such a detailed story for these two small features
concerns.summary: The whole interpretation rests on two weak in-gap features, and the referee asks why they are not more prominent.

concerns.quote: Is it possible these peaks are graphene LLs that are misinterpreted?... Could these two peaks be N=1 or 2 LLs, or N=2 or 3, for example. If not, why are the graphene LLs not observed
concerns.summary: The peaks could be graphene Landau levels rather than FGT states, and the absence of other Landau levels needs explaining.

concerns.quote: their DFT bandstructure calculation of FGT shows that the gamma point also has zero states like graphene and so one would expect FGT to display zero dI/dV signal at low voltage biases as well.
concerns.summary: FGT also has no states at Γ, so the claim that tunnelling into FGT can bypass graphene's gap needs justification.
concerns.response: addressed with new data or analysis

concerns.quote: Elastic tunneling into graphene is possible and would serve as an important check on the nature of the features observed... The authors should comment on the nature of their peak features for an elastic tunneling response.
concerns.summary: The authors should check the peaks against elastic tunnelling into graphene, where FGT-derived features should be absent.

concerns.quote: The presence of peaks could then be attributed to quantum dot (QD) states from the tip gating effect... The authors need to rule out that the peaks seen in their experiments are not related to QD states
concerns.summary: Raising the setpoint enhances elastic tunnelling into graphene, so the peaks and their field responses might be tip-induced graphene quantum-dot states rather than interface magnetic moments.

concerns.quote: The tip gating electric field is much larger than the gate electric field from conventional device architectures. This makes the authors finding less broadly applicable.
concerns.summary: The interfacial fields produced by tip gating may be unreachable in real devices, which limits applicability.

concerns.quote: Magnetic and electric field tunable orbital magnetic moments have been seen before see works by Y. Lee et al. PRL 2020, Z. Ge et al. PRL 2021, and Z. Ge et al., Nature Nanotechnology 2023.
concerns.summary: Field-tunable orbital moments in graphene have been reported before, and the manuscript must cite and compare with that work.

first_round.quote: The authors have made a good case for the explanation with the support of theoretical calculations. Overall, the paper is novel in characterizing an electrically controlled interphase magnetism.

I cannot recommend publication of this work in Nature Communications in its current stage. Below I elaborate on my criticisms and can consider this manuscript again if the authors address my criticisms.

recommendations.note: There is no sign of a transfer from another journal; Version 0 is the first round. R1 gives no explicit verdict. Their report is positive and asks only for clarifications (origin of the tunneling gap, why the features are small, ruling out Landau levels), so I inferred minor revision. R2 declines publication 'in its current stage' but offers to reconsider. They raise substantive challenges, such as how FGT is accessed given zero states at Gamma and ruling out tip-induced quantum-dot states, and ask for comparison with prior work. I read this as major revision rather than reject. Both referees recommended publication in Version 1.
recommendations.label: contested
